claim: Human iPSC-derived neurons proceed through initial neurodevelopmental stages 1-3 similar to dissociated rat neurons.
source: We first systematically assessed if the human iPSC-derived neurons proceed through the initial neurodevelopmental stages, which have previously been described in dissociated rat neurons (Dotti et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence characterization showing stage-specific markers and morphological changes, with citation to previous work in rat neurons.

claim: hiPSC-derived neuron cultures were obtained by neuronal induction of neuronal stem cells (NSCs) and maintained up to ~15 days.
source: The hiPSC-derived neuron cultures were obtained by neuronal induction of neuronal stem cells (NSCs) and maintained up to ~15 days.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methodology.

claim: Differentiated neurons adopted a cortical identity, as shown by the appearance of cortical marker Ctip2 in ß3-Tubulin positive cells.
source: Differentiated neurons adopted a cortical identity, as shown by the appearance of cortical marker Ctip2 in ß3-Tubulin positive cells specifically (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing co-localization of cortical and neuronal markers.

claim: NSC markers Nestin and Sox2 reduced over time during neuronal differentiation.
source: NSC markers Nestin and Sox2 reduced over time, while neuron marker ß3-Tubulin and axon markers Trim46 and Gap43 increased as cells differentiated and polarized (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing temporal changes in protein expression.

claim: Neuron marker ß3-Tubulin and axon markers Trim46 and Gap43 increased as cells differentiated and polarized.
source: NSC markers Nestin and Sox2 reduced over time, while neuron marker ß3-Tubulin and axon markers Trim46 and Gap43 increased as cells differentiated and polarized (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing temporal changes in protein expression.

claim: The timing of AIS assembly occurred at day ~13-14.
source: Accordingly, the timing of AIS assembly at day ~13–14 coincided with an observed developmental decrease of axon width, whereas dendrite width remained unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and morphological measurements.

claim: AIS assembly at day ~13-14 coincided with a developmental decrease of axon width.
source: Accordingly, the timing of AIS assembly at day ~13–14 coincided with an observed developmental decrease of axon width, whereas dendrite width remained unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by morphological measurements showing changes in axon width.

claim: Dendrite width remained unaffected during AIS assembly.
source: Accordingly, the timing of AIS assembly at day ~13–14 coincided with an observed developmental decrease of axon width, whereas dendrite width remained unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by morphological measurements showing no change in dendrite width.

claim: hiPSC-derived NSCs follow a relatively prolonged neuronal and axonal development compared to dissociated rat neurons.
source: These observations indicate that hiPSC-derived NSCs follow a relatively prolonged neuronal and axonal development compared to dissociated rat neurons, consistent with the protracted development of the human brain (Dotti et al., 1988; Petanjek et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference from timing data compared to literature on rat neurons, with citations to support protracted human development.

claim: Trim46 and AnkG localization largely overlapped in the AIS.
source: Consistent with previous reports in dissociated rat neurons, we found that Trim46 and AnkG localization largely overlapped, with the peak of AnkG intensity located ~6 µm more distally than the peak Trim46 intensity (Figure 1F,G; van Beuningen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity profiles and citation to previous work.

claim: The peak of AnkG intensity was located ~6 µm more distally than the peak Trim46 intensity in the AIS.
source: Consistent with previous reports in dissociated rat neurons, we found that Trim46 and AnkG localization largely overlapped, with the peak of AnkG intensity located ~6 µm more distally than the peak Trim46 intensity (Figure 1F,G; van Beuningen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity profiles.

claim: The AIS structure was enriched for voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV), which strongly overlapped with AnkG structures.
source: The AIS structure was also enriched for voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV), which strongly overlapped with AnkG structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing co-localization.

claim: AP firing was observed upon positive somatic current stimulation in nearly all recorded neurons (59/61).
source: We observed AP firing upon positive somatic current stimulation in nearly all recorded neurons (59/61).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology recordings.

claim: 22 neurons (41%) fired multiple times upon higher current stimulation.
source: Of these, 22 neurons (41%) fired multiple times upon higher current stimulation, while 32 neurons (59%) fired only once, independent of stimulus strength (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology recordings and quantification.

claim: 32 neurons (59%) fired only once, independent of stimulus strength.
source: Of these, 22 neurons (41%) fired multiple times upon higher current stimulation, while 32 neurons (59%) fired only once, independent of stimulus strength (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology recordings and quantification.

claim: Neurons that fired a single AP showed more immature intrinsic cell properties, including depolarized resting membrane potential, lower input resistance, smaller maximum sodium current and smaller after-hyperpolarization.
source: Neurons that fired a single AP showed more immature intrinsic cell properties, including depolarized resting membrane potential, lower input resistance, smaller maximum sodium current and smaller after-hyperpolarization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements comparing single vs. multiple AP firing neurons.

claim: Spontaneous AP firing or incoming spontaneous synaptic responses were only observed in a few neurons (4/22).
source: Spontaneous AP firing or incoming spontaneous synaptic responses were only observed in a few neurons (4/22).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology recordings.

claim: Synapse formation typically starts around two weeks after neuronal induction in human iPSC-derived neurons.
source: This is in line with previous studies reporting that synapse formation typically starts around two weeks after neuronal induction in human iPSC-derived neurons (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 14,551 transcripts were identified by RNA sequencing.
source: In two biological replicates with two technical replicates each, we identified transcripts corresponding to 14,551 genes by RNA sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: 9655 transcripts were successfully quantified at all time points.
source: Of these, 9655 transcripts were successfully quantified at all time points and normalized to reads per million for further analysis (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: 614 genes were downregulated at day 7 compared to day 1.
source: As expected, most genes with significantly altered expression were found between day 1 and day 7: 614 genes were downregulated and 549 genes were upregulated at day 7 compared to day 1 (FDR < 0.05 [Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—source data 3]).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: 549 genes were upregulated at day 7 compared to day 1.
source: As expected, most genes with significantly altered expression were found between day 1 and day 7: 614 genes were downregulated and 549 genes were upregulated at day 7 compared to day 1 (FDR < 0.05 [Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—source data 3]).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Downregulated genes are enriched for GO terms related to cell proliferation, such as DNA replication, cell cycle, and cell division.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of downregulated genes indicates that many of the top enriched GO terms relate to processes involved in cell proliferation, such as DNA replication, cell cycle, and cell division (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Upregulated genes correspond to cellular components and biological processes including nervous system development, neuron projection, and axonogenesis.
source: Upregulated genes correspond to several cellular components and biological processes including nervous system development, neuron projection, and axonogenesis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Upregulated genes showed enrichment of multiple GO terms related to the microtubule cytoskeleton.
source: Interestingly, upregulated genes also showed enrichment of multiple GO terms related to the microtubule cytoskeleton (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Upregulation of many genes related to neurodevelopment and axonogenesis was previously observed in differentiating mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and iPSCs as well as human ESCs.
source: Consistently, upregulation of many genes related to neurodevelopment and axonogenesis was previously observed in differentiating mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and iPSCs as well as human ESCs (Wu et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SOX2, NOTCH1, and OTX2 were among the highly downregulated genes.
source: Among the highly downregulated genes were several proliferation factors, such as SOX2, NOTCH1, and OTX2 (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: The chromokinesin motor proteins KIF4a and KIF22, involved in cell proliferation through regulation of spindle microtubule dynamics during mitosis, were downregulated.
source: Furthermore, the chromokinesin motor proteins KIF4a and KIF22, involved in cell proliferation through regulation of spindle microtubule dynamics during mitosis, were downregulated (Almeida and Maiato, 2018; Bisht et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and citation to literature on protein function.

claim: Genes of several neuronal and axonal kinesins were upregulated, including KIF1a, KIF5c, and KIF21b.
source: Conversely, genes of several neuronal and axonal kinesins were upregulated, including KIF1a, KIF5c, and KIF21b (Figure 2—source data 3; Hirokawa and Tanaka, 2015).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and citation to literature.

claim: The neuron-specific tubulin TUBB3 and the axonal microtubule associated protein MAPT were upregulated.
source: Additionally, the neuron-specific tubulin TUBB3 and the axonal microtubule associated protein MAPT were upregulated (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: 7512 proteins were identified in two technical replicates by mass spectrometry.
source: We identified 7512 proteins in two technical replicates and quantified 5620 proteins across all three time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data.

claim: 5620 proteins were quantified across all three time points.
source: We identified 7512 proteins in two technical replicates and quantified 5620 proteins across all three time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data.

claim: 2218 proteins showed a changed expression profile during differentiation and neurodevelopment.
source: Of these, 2218 proteins showed a changed expression profile during differentiation and neurodevelopment.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data analysis.

claim: Six clusters with distinct expression profiles were identified by unsupervised clustering of proteome data.
source: We assessed the global proteome changes by unsupervised clustering, and identified six clusters with distinct expression profiles (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of proteomics data.

claim: Cluster 1 contains proteins that show a slight increase from day 1 to day 7.
source: Cluster 1 contains proteins that show a slight increase from day 1 to day 7.
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of proteomics data.

claim: Cluster 1 shows GO enrichment of terms related to neuronal differentiation and intracellular transport mechanisms.
source: GO enrichment analysis revealed enrichment of several terms related to neuronal differentiation and intracellular transport mechanisms, which reflects cell-autonomous remodeling of molecular processes (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of proteomics data.

claim: KLC1, a subunit of the microtubule motor protein required for neuronal differentiation from human embryonic stem cells, is upregulated in cluster 1.
source: One of the upregulated proteins in cluster one is KLC1, a subunit of the microtubule motor protein, which was found to be required for neuronal differentiation from human embryonic stem cells (Killian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data and citation to literature on protein function.

claim: The AIS protein Trim46, which regulates neuronal polarity and axon specification by controlling microtubule organization during development, is found in cluster 1.
source: The AIS protein Trim46, which is known to regulate neuronal polarity and axon specification by controlling microtubule organization during development, is also found in this cluster (van Beuningen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data and citation to literature on protein function.

claim: Cluster 1 contains Camsap1, Camsap2 and Camsap3, proteins which localize to the minus ends of microtubules to stabilize them, thereby regulating neuronal polarity.
source: Furthermore, this cluster contains Camsap1, Camsap2 and Camsap3, proteins which localize to the minus ends of microtubules to stabilize them, thereby regulating neuronal polarity (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data and citation to literature on protein function.

claim: Proteins in cluster 2 present a considerable increase in relative expression from day 3 to day 7, which coincides with the onset of axon formation and development (stage 3).
source: Proteins in cluster 2 present a considerable increase in relative expression from day 3 to day 7, which coincides with the onset of axon formation and development (stage 3).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data and temporal correlation with developmental stages.

claim: Cluster 2 shows enriched GO terms including proteins associated with neuronal development, axonogenesis, and other axon-related mechanisms.
source: Accordingly, enriched GO terms include proteins associated with neuronal development, axonogenesis, and other axon-related mechanisms (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of proteomics data.

claim: GO terms representing factors associated with neuronal development, axons, and synapses were enriched during differentiation of immortalized human neural progenitor cells.
source: Similarly, the GO terms representing factors associated with neuronal development, axons, and synapses were also enriched during differentiation of immortalized human neural progenitor cells (Song et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Several members of the Septin family (neuronal-specific Sept3, Sept5, and Sept6) are among the highly upregulated proteins in cluster 2.
source: Among the highly upregulated proteins in this cluster are several members of the Septin family: neuronal-specific Sept3, Sept5, and Sept6 (Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data.

claim: Emerging evidence implicates Septins as potential factors for establishing neuronal polarity.
source: Although mechanistic insights remain unclear, emerging evidence implicates Septins as potential factors for establishing neuronal polarity (Falk et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature.

claim: Septins interact with actin and microtubule networks and could affect neuronal polarity by regulating cytoskeleton dynamics.
source: Septins interact with actin and microtubule networks and could affect neuronal polarity by regulating cytoskeleton dynamics (Spiliotis, 2018; Falk et al., 2019 ).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature with speculative language ('could affect').

claim: Sept6 is suggested to play a role in axonal filopodia formation as well as in dendritic branching.
source: Sept6 specifically is suggested to play a role in axonal filopodia formation as well as in dendritic branching, and its increased expression coincides with axonal outgrowth (Cho et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2012 ).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature.

claim: Sept6 increased expression coincides with axonal outgrowth.
source: Sept6 specifically is suggested to play a role in axonal filopodia formation as well as in dendritic branching, and its increased expression coincides with axonal outgrowth (Cho et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2012 ).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature and temporal correlation.

claim: DCX, Tau, Ncam1, Basp1, Snap91, and Syt1 are proteins with the highest relative expression in cluster 2 and are generally considered to be neuronal differentiation and polarization markers.
source: Moreover, examples of proteins with the highest relative expression in this cluster are DCX, Tau, Ncam1, Basp1, Snap91, and Syt1, which are generally considered to be neuronal differentiation and polarization markers (Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data and established knowledge about these markers.

claim: Cluster 3 represents proteins with increased expression from day 1 to day 3, and minimal changes in expression from day 3 to day 7.
source: Cluster 3 represents proteins with increased expression from day 1 to day 3, and minimal changes in expression from day 3 to day 7.
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of proteomics data.

claim: Cluster 3 comprises proteins enriched in GO terms associated with cell metabolism and (re)localization of intracellular and extracellular components.
source: This cluster comprises proteins enriched in GO terms that are associated with cell metabolism and (re)localization of intracellular and extracellular components, which correspond to substantial changes in the cellular proteome (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of proteomics data.

claim: Sox4 and Sox11, both members of the SoxC transcription factor family, show differential expression from day 1 to day 3 in cluster 3.
source: Proteins in this cluster that show differential expression from day 1 to day 3 include Sox4 and Sox11, both members of the SoxC transcription factor family (Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data.

claim: Sox4 and Sox11 are involved in neurogenesis and their expression induces subsequent expression of neuron-specific genes.
source: These factors are involved in neurogenesis and their expression induces subsequent expression of neuron-specific genes (Kavyanifar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on protein function.

claim: Arpc2 and Arpc4, subunits of the Arp2/3 complex, are represented in cluster 3.
source: Also represented in this cluster are Arpc2 and Arpc4, subunits of the Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: Supported by proteomics data.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex mediates actin polymerization and is required for formation of lamellipodia and filopodia as well as axon guidance.
source: The Arp2/3 complex mediates actin polymerization and is required for formation of lamellipodia and filopodia as well as axon guidance (Chou and Wang, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on protein function.

claim: Clusters 4, 5, and 6 encompass proteins that are downregulated during the differentiation of NSCs into polarized neurons.
source: Clusters 4, 5, and 6 encompass proteins that are downregulated during the differentiation of NSCs into polarized neurons.
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of proteomics data.

claim: GO analysis of clusters 4, 5, and 6 reveals they contain proteins involved in intracellular metabolism and homeostasis, genomic translation, the cell cycle, and biosynthesis of amino acids and peptides.
source: GO analysis of these clusters reveals that they contain proteins involved in intracellular metabolism and homeostasis, genomic translation, the cell cycle, and biosynthesis of amino acids and peptides (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of proteomics data.

claim: Downregulation of DNA replication and cell cycle-related proteins coincides with terminal differentiation in neuroblastoma cells and with development of cultured rat neurons.
source: Downregulation of DNA replication and cell cycle-related proteins is also reported to coincide with terminal differentiation in neuroblastoma cells and with development of cultured rat neurons (Murillo et al., 2017; Frese et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 4536 factors followed the same trend for transcriptomic and proteomic expression dynamics out of 7021 compared factors.
source: Based on their annotated gene names we were able to compare the expression dynamics of 7021 factors. Of these, 4536 followed the same trend for transcriptomic and proteomic expression dynamics, and overall, we found a significant correlation between the relative transcriptomic and proteomic expression profiles (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by correlative analysis of transcriptomics and proteomics data.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the relative transcriptomic and proteomic expression profiles.
source: Based on their annotated gene names we were able to compare the expression dynamics of 7021 factors. Of these, 4536 followed the same trend for transcriptomic and proteomic expression dynamics, and overall, we found a significant correlation between the relative transcriptomic and proteomic expression profiles (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by correlative analysis showing R = 0.51, p<0.0001.

claim: Typical stem cell markers (NOTCH1, SOX2, MKI67, LIN28A, OTX2, and NES) showed a downregulation of both RNA and protein levels during neuronal differentiation.
source: In agreement with the observed immunofluorescence, typical stem cell markers (NOTCH1, SOX2, MKI67, LIN28A, OTX2, and NES) showed a downregulation of both RNA and protein levels during neuronal differentiation.
evidence: Supported by transcriptomics and proteomics data.

claim: RNA levels as well as protein levels of typical neuron markers (DCX, ENO2, SYP, MAP2, STMN1, and TUBB3) displayed a marked increase during neuronal development.
source: RNA levels as well as protein levels of typical neuron markers (DCX, ENO2, SYP, MAP2, STMN1, and TUBB3) and of axonal markers (TRIM46, MAPT, BASP1, ANK3, NCAM1, GAP43, and NFASC) displayed a marked increase during neuronal development (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomics and proteomics data.

claim: RNA levels as well as protein levels of axonal markers (TRIM46, MAPT, BASP1, ANK3, NCAM1, GAP43, and NFASC) displayed a marked increase during neuronal development.
source: RNA levels as well as protein levels of typical neuron markers (DCX, ENO2, SYP, MAP2, STMN1, and TUBB3) and of axonal markers (TRIM46, MAPT, BASP1, ANK3, NCAM1, GAP43, and NFASC) displayed a marked increase during neuronal development (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomics and proteomics data.

claim: Dynamic developmental expression profiles were observed for several semaphorins and Rap1GTPases, which are important regulators of neuronal polarity and migration in the developing mammalian neocortex.
source: Dynamic developmental expression profiles were also observed for several semaphorins and Rap1GTPases, which are important regulators of neuronal polarity and migration in the developing mammalian neocortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E; Pasterkamp, 2012; Shah et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomics and proteomics data with citation to literature on protein function.

claim: In stage 2 neurons, AIS proteins Trim46 and AnkG appeared as punctate structures at one or more neurites in a subset of neurons.
source: In stage 2 neurons, in which neurites are unpolarized and have similar lengths, AIS proteins Trim46 and AnkG appeared as punctate structures at one or more neurites in a subset of neurons (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: There is a developmental transition over time from stage 2a to stage 2b neurons.
source: Quantification of the relative abundance of stage 2 neurons lacking AIS proteins (referred to as stage 2a), or containing AIS proteins at one or more neurites (referred to as stage 2b), showed a developmental transition over time from stage 2a to stage 2b neurons (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data over time.

claim: AIS proteins in stage 3 neurons first appeared as noncontinuous structures consisting of multiple smaller puncta and stretches that cover distal parts of the axon (stage 3a), prior to their localization in the AIS at the proximal axon (stage 3b).
source: Interestingly, we found that AIS proteins in stage 3 neurons first appeared as noncontinuous structures consisting of multiple smaller puncta and stretches that cover distal parts of the axon (referred to as stage 3a), prior to their more conventional localization in the AIS at the proximal axon (referred to as stage 3b) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing spatial distribution of AIS proteins.

claim: The newly identified axon developmental stage 3a was also observed in neurons differentiated using other protocols and in neurons derived from other donors.
source: This newly identified axon developmental stage 3a was also observed in neurons differentiated using other protocols and in neurons derived from other donors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from multiple differentiation protocols and donor cell lines.

claim: There is a developmental decline of stage 2b neurons accompanied with an increase of stage 3a neurons, as well as an increase of stage 3b neurons with a relatively later onset.
source: Quantifications of the abundance of these neurodevelopmental stages over time revealed a developmental decline of stage 2b neurons that was accompanied with an increase of stage 3a neurons, as well as an increase of stage 3b neurons with a relatively later onset (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data over time.

claim: The total neurite length covered by Trim46 or AnkG signals was strongly increased by ~40% in stage 3a neurons.
source: Developmental changes in the length of AnkG and Trim46 structures were observed, as the total neurite length covered by Trim46 or AnkG signals was strongly increased by ~40% in stage 3a neurons, and significantly reduced by ~55% in stage 3b neurons (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of immunofluorescence data.

claim: The total neurite length covered by Trim46 or AnkG signals was significantly reduced by ~55% in stage 3b neurons.
source: Developmental changes in the length of AnkG and Trim46 structures were observed, as the total neurite length covered by Trim46 or AnkG signals was strongly increased by ~40% in stage 3a neurons, and significantly reduced by ~55% in stage 3b neurons (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of immunofluorescence data.

claim: The axonal Trim46 and AnkG structures were localized more distally in stage 3a neurons, as the distance from the soma to both the start as well as the end of the Trim46 and AnkG appearance was significantly larger compared to stage 3b neurons.
source: Movereover, the axonal Trim46 and AnkG structures were localized more distally in stage 3a neurons, as the distance from the soma to both the start as well as the end of the Trim46 and AnkG appearance was significantly larger compared to stage 3b neurons (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of immunofluorescence data.

claim: The localization of NaV at axons shows a similar dynamic profile as Trim46 and AnkG during development.
source: The localization of NaV at axons shows a similar dynamic profile as Trim46 and AnkG during development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Axon specification (transition stage 2–3) in human iPSC-derived neurons can be subdivided in four steps (stage 2a, 2b, 3a and 3b) based on the subcellular localization of AIS proteins.
source: Together, these data imply that axon specification (transition stage 2–3) in human iPSC-derived neurons can be subdivided in four steps (stage 2a, 2b, 3a and 3b) based on the subcellular localization of AIS proteins.
evidence: Inference from immunofluorescence data showing distinct spatial patterns of AIS proteins.

claim: AIS proteins first form relatively long, noncontinuous structures in the distal axon (stage 3a) before accumulating at the proximal axon to form the AIS structure (stage 3b).
source: Specifically, AIS proteins first form relatively long, noncontinuous structures in the distal axon (stage 3a) before accumulating at the proximal axon to form the AIS structure (stage 3b).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing temporal and spatial changes in AIS protein localization.

claim: Neurons recorded on day 13–14 fired APs with a larger amplitude and shorter half-width compared to 10–11 days old neurons.
source: Neurons recorded on day 13–14 fired APs with a larger amplitude and shorter half-width compared to 10–11 days old neurons (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements.

claim: No differences in AP amplitude and half-width were found between neurons of 7 and 10–11 days.
source: No differences in AP amplitude and half-width were found between neurons of 7 and 10–11 days.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements.

claim: On day 7, neurons fired APs with smaller after-hyperpolarization.
source: However, on day 7, neurons fired APs with smaller after-hyperpolarization (data not shown), possibly reflecting a developmental increase in potassium channels (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements with citation to literature for interpretation.

claim: Other intrinsic properties, like resting membrane potential, input resistance, AP firing threshold and maximum sodium current, remained stable during the developmental period from day 7 to 14.
source: Other intrinsic properties, like resting membrane potential, input resistance, AP firing threshold and maximum sodium current, remained stable during this developmental period.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology measurements.

claim: There is a developmental maturation of specific AP properties, which coincides with the timing of the developmental transition from stage 3a to stage 3b neurons.
source: Together, these results indicate a developmental maturation of specific AP properties, which coincides with the timing of the developmental transition from stage 3a to stage 3b neurons.
evidence: Inference from temporal correlation between electrophysiology and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Bidirectional MT+TIP movement was observed at day 5 (representing stage 2 neurons) with a preference for the anterograde direction.
source: Bidirectional MT+TIP movement, as shown by comets moving in both the anterograde and retrograde direction, was observed at day 5 (representing stage 2 neurons) with a preference for the anterograde direction (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data.

claim: Over time, the preference for anterograde MT+TIP movement shifted towards more retrograde movement in developing dendrites, and towards unidirectional anterograde movement in developing axons.
source: Over time, this preference shifted towards more retrograde movement in developing dendrites, and towards unidirectional anterograde movement in developing axons (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data over time.

claim: These changes in MT+TIP directionality are consistent with differences in microtubule organization in axons and dendrites found in non-human neurons.
source: These changes are consistent with differences in microtubule organization in axons and dendrites found in non-human neurons (Yau et al., 2016; Schätzle et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The shift towards a unidirectional microtubule organization in axons occurred first in distal parts of the axon, followed by proximal reorganization at later time points.
source: In similar fashion to the distal to proximal reorganization of AIS proteins (Figure 3), the observed shift towards a unidirectional microtubule organization in axons occurred first in distal parts of the axon, followed by proximal reorganization at later time points.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data showing spatial and temporal patterns.

claim: The observed developmental changes in anterograde and retrograde ratios are mostly explained by changes in retrograde comets, as the total number of retrograde comets over time was increased in dendrites and decreased in axons.
source: The observed developmental changes in anterograde and retrograde ratios are mostly explained by changes in retrograde comets, as the total number of retrograde comets over time was increased in dendrites and decreased in axons (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of live-cell imaging data.

claim: The comet growth speed is slightly reduced during development.
source: The comet growth speed is slightly reduced during development, while comet run length increased markedly, suggesting a reduction in catastrophe events during axon and dendrite development (Figure 4G,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of live-cell imaging data.

claim: Comet run length increased markedly during development, suggesting a reduction in catastrophe events during axon and dendrite development.
source: The comet growth speed is slightly reduced during development, while comet run length increased markedly, suggesting a reduction in catastrophe events during axon and dendrite development (Figure 4G,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of live-cell imaging data with inference about catastrophe events.

claim: Following laser severing, a strong shift towards a balanced, bidirectional orientation in developing dendrites is observed.
source: Following laser severing, a strong shift towards a balanced, bidirectional orientation in developing dendrites is observed (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by laser-severing experiments and live-cell imaging data.

claim: The number of comets in both directions increased during development in dendrites, with those moving in the retrograde direction increasing relatively more.
source: The number of comets in both directions increased during development, with those moving in the retrograde direction increasing relatively more (Figure 4L,M).
evidence: Supported by quantification of laser-severing experiments.

claim: The increase in retrograde comets after laser severing in dendrites suggests the presence of a larger pool of stable, minus-end out microtubules in dendrites.
source: This suggests the presence of a larger pool of stable, minus-end out microtubules in dendrites.
evidence: Inference from laser-severing experiments showing increased retrograde comets.

claim: In developing axons, the shift towards unidirectional, plus-end out microtubules was more notably observed following laser severing.
source: In developing axons, the shift towards unidirectional, plus-end out microtubules was more notably observed following laser severing (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by laser-severing experiments and live-cell imaging data.

claim: Laser severing led to a large increase in the number of anterogradely moving comets in axons, suggesting the presence of a stable pool of plus-end out microtubules.
source: Laser severing led to a large increase in the number of anterogradely moving comets (Figure 4L), suggesting the presence of a stable pool of plus-end out microtubules.
evidence: Inference from laser-severing experiments showing increased anterograde comets.

claim: The axonal microtubule remodeling in a distal to proximal fashion coincides with the observed relocation of AIS proteins.
source: These results indicate that the axonal microtubule remodeling in a distal to proximal fashion coincides with the observed relocation of AIS proteins.
evidence: Inference from temporal and spatial correlation between microtubule dynamics and AIS protein localization.

claim: Axon formation is characterized by the reorganization of the axonal microtubule network and relocation of the AIS from the distal to proximal axon.
source: Together, these data show that axon formation is characterized by the reorganization of the axonal microtubule network and relocation of the AIS from the distal to proximal axon (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Synthesis of multiple lines of evidence from immunofluorescence and live-cell imaging data.

claim: Human iPSC-derived neurons develop at slower rates than non-human neurons.
source: Non-human neurons develop at faster rates: for example, rat dissociated neurons reach stage 3 after approximately 1.5 days in culture, and cortical development and maturation in mammals ranging from mouse to primate is both faster and less complex than in humans (Dotti et al., 1988; Clowry et al., 2010; Molnár and Clowry, 2012; Silbereis et al., 2016; Marchetto et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature comparing developmental timing across species.

claim: Rat dissociated neurons reach stage 3 after approximately 1.5 days in culture.
source: Non-human neurons develop at faster rates: for example, rat dissociated neurons reach stage 3 after approximately 1.5 days in culture, and cortical development and maturation in mammals ranging from mouse to primate is both faster and less complex than in humans (Dotti et al., 1988; Clowry et al., 2010; Molnár and Clowry, 2012; Silbereis et al., 2016; Marchetto et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature.

claim: Human iPSC-derived neurons transit to stage 3 in approximately 7–14 days.
source: We found that human iPSC-derived neurons transit to stage 3 in approximately 7–14 days, which is consistent with the described prolonged development of human neurons in vivo and in vitro (Grabrucker et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and citation to literature.

claim: Co-culturing with astrocytes could promote synaptogenesis, as this has been shown to enhance synaptic connectivity.
source: Notably, co-culturing with astrocytes could promote synaptogenesis, as this has been shown to enhance synaptic connectivity (Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to literature.

claim: The prolonged development of human iPSC-derived neurons allows studying neurobiological processes, such as AP maturation and AIS assembly, with higher temporal resolution.
source: The prolonged development of human iPSC-derived neurons allows studying neurobiological processes, such as AP maturation and AIS assembly, with higher temporal resolution.
evidence: Inference from the observed slower developmental timeline.

claim: 1163 transcripts showed differential expression during early neuronal development.
source: We established transcriptomic and proteomic profiles of the early developmental stages (stage 1–3), comprising 14,551 transcripts and 7512 protein identifications, of which we assessed 1163 and 2218 factors that showed differential expression, respectively.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: 2218 proteins showed differential expression during early neuronal development.
source: We established transcriptomic and proteomic profiles of the early developmental stages (stage 1–3), comprising 14,551 transcripts and 7512 protein identifications, of which we assessed 1163 and 2218 factors that showed differential expression, respectively.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data analysis.

claim: Transcriptomic and proteomic profiles point to the importance of microtubule cytoskeleton remodeling in the early stage of neuronal development.
source: These transcriptomic and proteomic profiles point to the importance of microtubule cytoskeleton remodeling in the early stage of neuronal development.
evidence: Inference from GO enrichment analysis of transcriptomics and proteomics data.

claim: A distinct, previously unrecognized developmental stage during early axon development was identified, characterized by the reorganization of the axonal microtubule network and relocation of AIS proteins from the distal to proximal axon.
source: Specifically, we identified a distinct, previously unrecognized developmental stage during early axon development, characterized by the reorganization of the axonal microtubule network and relocation of AIS proteins from the distal to proximal axon.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and live-cell imaging data showing novel spatial and temporal patterns.

claim: The transition through early axon developmental stages coincided with the time window in which maturation of action potentials occurred.
source: The transition through these early axon developmental stages coincided with the time window in which maturation of action potentials occurred.
evidence: Inference from temporal correlation between immunofluorescence and electrophysiology data.

claim: MT+TIP growth speeds in human neurons are higher than those found in rodent neurons in vitro and in vivo.
source: We also observed differences in microtubule dynamics, as MT+TIP growth speeds are higher than those found in rodent neurons in vitro and in vivo, hinting at species-specific regulation of microtubule dynamics in human neurons (Stepanova et al., 2003; Kleele et al., 2014; Yau et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data and citation to literature for comparison.

claim: Species-specific regulation of microtubule dynamics may exist in human neurons.
source: We also observed differences in microtubule dynamics, as MT+TIP growth speeds are higher than those found in rodent neurons in vitro and in vivo, hinting at species-specific regulation of microtubule dynamics in human neurons (Stepanova et al., 2003; Kleele et al., 2014; Yau et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative inference from comparison with literature data.

claim: The AIS is required for generating action potentials (APs) and maintaining neuronal polarity.
source: The AIS is required for generating action potentials (APs) and maintaining neuronal polarity.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about AIS function.

claim: Trim46 localizes to the AIS and is critical for axon formation by forming parallel microtubule bundles in the proximal axon.
source: In addition to the classic AIS component Ankyrin-G (AnkG), the microtubule binding protein Trim46 also localizes to the AIS and is critical for axon formation by forming parallel microtubule bundles in the proximal axon (van Beuningen et al., 2015; Gumy et al., 2017; Harterink et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: AnkG can act as a scaffold to recruit Trim46-positive microtubules and subsequently direct AIS protein trafficking to the proximal axon.
source: It has been shown that AnkG can act as a scaffold to recruit Trim46-positive microtubules and subsequently direct AIS protein trafficking to the proximal axon (Fréal et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: AnkG and Trim46 cooperate to form a stable AIS-microtubule structure in the proximal axon through a feedback-based mechanism.
source: Recently Fréal et al., 2019, described a feedback-based mechanism that drives AIS assembly, in which membrane, scaffolding, and microtubule(-associated) proteins, including AnkG and Trim46, cooperate to form a stable AIS-microtubule structure in the proximal axon.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The possible function of AIS proteins in the distal axon remains elusive.
source: The possible function of AIS proteins in the distal axon remains elusive.
evidence: Statement acknowledging lack of knowledge.

claim: AIS proteins present at the distal axon may assist in locally stabilizing microtubules to presumably drive axon outgrowth.
source: Similar to their function in stabilizing microtubules at the proximal axon, the AIS proteins present at the distal axon may also assist in locally stabilizing microtubules to presumably drive axon outgrowth.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on known function at proximal axon.

claim: AnkG in distal axons may provide additional support to the formation of Trim46-positive parallel microtubules during outgrowth.
source: AnkG in distal axons may provide additional support to the formation of Trim46-positive parallel microtubules during outgrowth.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis.

claim: As Trim46 moves proximally, the axonal microtubule network close to the cell body is also remodeled to the characteristic uniform plus-end out orientation.
source: Then, as Trim46 moves proximally, the axonal microtubule network close to the cell body is also remodeled to the characteristic uniform plus-end out orientation.
evidence: Inference from observed spatial and temporal patterns of Trim46 localization and microtubule organization.

claim: It remains unknown if the observed intermediate step of distal AIS protein accumulation is unique to human neurons.
source: It remains unknown if the observed intermediate step of distal AIS protein accumulation is unique to human neurons.
evidence: Statement acknowledging lack of knowledge.

claim: Axons in humans grow significantly longer compared to rodents, thus additional regulatory mechanisms enhancing axon outgrowth might be at play in humans.
source: Axons in humans grow significantly longer compared to rodents, thus additional regulatory mechanisms enhancing axon outgrowth might be at play in humans.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on known anatomical differences.

claim: It is possible that the intermediate step of distal AIS protein accumulation has not been observed in rodent neurons because of their relatively faster development.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that these changes have not been observed in rodent neurons because of their relatively faster development.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis.
